items.question: Genetically modified and genome-edited crops promise higher yields and climate resilience, yet remain contentious in India. Critically examine the regulatory framework and recent developments, with the debate over GM mustard and the 2025 genome-edited rice varieties.
items.modelAnswer:
India's approach to modern crop biotechnology balances the promise of **food security and climate resilience** against **biosafety, ecological and socio-economic concerns**. The **regulatory framework** rests on the **Rules of 1989** under the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**, administered chiefly by the **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)** under the **MoEFCC**, with the **RCGM** (under DBT) overseeing research and confined trials.

The **current status** is cautious: **Bt cotton** (approved 2002) remains the **only commercially cultivated GM crop**; **Bt brinjal**, though cleared in 2009, has been under a **moratorium since 2010**; and **GM mustard (DMH-11)**, recommended for environmental release by GEAC in 2022, drew a **Supreme Court split verdict in 2024**, with the Court directing the government to frame a **national policy on GM crops** after wide consultation. Objections centre on **long-term safety data**, effects on **pollinators and biodiversity**, **herbicide use**, and **farmer dependence on seed companies**.

A distinct turn came in **May 2025** with India's **first genome-edited rice varieties — DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala)** (ICAR-IIRR) and **Pusa DST Rice 1** (ICAR-IARI). Created through **SDN-1/SDN-2 editing** that leaves **no foreign DNA**, they were **exempted from GM biosafety rules** (2022 notification) and promise higher yield with lower water and fertiliser use.

**Way forward**: a transparent, science-based, and **participatory GM policy**, robust post-release monitoring, clear labelling, and strengthened public-sector research so benefits reach farmers — including in agrarian states like **Andhra Pradesh** — without compromising biosafety.
keyPoints: Framework: Rules 1989 under EPA 1986; GEAC (MoEFCC) apex regulator, RCGM (DBT) for research/trials.
Bt cotton = only commercial GM crop; Bt brinjal under 2010 moratorium.
GM mustard DMH-11: GEAC release nod (2022); Supreme Court split verdict (2024) directed a national GM policy.
May 2025: first genome-edited rice — DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) & Pusa DST Rice 1 via SDN-1/SDN-2 (no foreign DNA, exempt).
Concerns: biosafety data, biodiversity/pollinators, herbicide use, seed dependence.
Way forward: transparent participatory policy, monitoring, labelling, strong public-sector research.
items.source: MoEFCC/GEAC; Supreme Court (2024); PIB & ICAR — genome-edited rice (2025)

items.question: Discuss how recent policy and institutional initiatives — the BioE3 Policy, BRIC and the Genome India Project — position biotechnology as a driver of India's economy, environment and employment.
items.modelAnswer:
Biotechnology has moved from a niche research field to a **strategic driver of growth**, and India's recent initiatives signal an ambition to build a **globally competitive bioeconomy**.

The **BioE3 Policy (2024)** — **Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment**, approved by the Union Cabinet and steered by the **DBT** — is the centrepiece. It promotes **high-performance biomanufacturing**, **biofoundries** and bio-AI hubs across thematic sectors such as **bio-based chemicals and enzymes, functional foods, precision biotherapeutics, climate-resilient agriculture, carbon capture, and marine/space biotech**. By substituting fossil-based production with **bio-based, circular processes**, it links directly to **net-zero** goals while creating skilled **green jobs**.

Institutionally, the **Biotechnology Research and Innovation Council (BRIC, 2024)** merged **14 autonomous DBT institutes** into one apex society, reducing fragmentation and enabling shared resources and mission-mode research; **BIRAC** continues to nurture **start-ups and innovation**.

On the science front, the **Genome India Project** (launched 2020, DBT-funded, with IISc's Centre for Brain Research) sequenced **10,000 Indian genomes** (completion announced in 2025), building an **Indian reference genome** for **precision medicine** and disease-risk prediction tailored to India's diversity.

Together these create a virtuous cycle — **research (GIP) → institutions (BRIC/BIRAC) → industry and jobs (BioE3)**. **Challenges** remain: scaling manufacturing, skilled talent, data privacy/ethics in genomics, and equitable access. Regional assets such as **AMTZ, Visakhapatnam** and the **Genome Valley** cluster can anchor this bioeconomy, provided regulation, funding and ethics keep pace.
keyPoints: BioE3 Policy (2024) = Biotechnology for Economy, Environment, Employment; DBT-led, high-performance biomanufacturing.
BioE3 links bio-based circular production to net-zero goals and green jobs.
BRIC (2024) merged 14 DBT institutes into one apex society; BIRAC supports start-ups.
Genome India Project (2020, DBT/IISc) sequenced 10,000 genomes (announced 2025) for precision medicine.
Challenges: scale-up, talent, genomic data privacy/ethics; AP assets AMTZ & Genome Valley can anchor it.
items.source: PIB / DBT — BioE3 Policy, BRIC; Genome India Project
